investigations.cluster: miter-limit, renamed: stroke-cull-centreline-bounds. The miter limit is not involved. femtovg drops a whole stroke when its centreline lies off the canvas, even if the stroke's width reaches onto it.
investigations.mechanism:
Canvas::stroke_path_internal (src/lib.rs:1547) culls the path with an early-out at src/lib.rs:1607-1614. That test compares path_cache.bounds against the canvas size (0..self.width(), 0..self.height()). Those bounds are the flattened centreline in device space. The test runs before the line width is known (it is computed at :1621) and before StrokeSettings::reach (src/paint.rs:457, used at :1640 for draw_clip). So any stroke whose centreline is entirely past one canvas edge is thrown away, even when its half-width, miter tip or square cap reaches back onto the canvas. The shadow code 20 lines above (:1578-1589) already says "The path-cache bounds only cover the centerline" and expands them. The cull does not. The early-out goes back to Peter Todorov's 2020 commits (227cb6c1, 66a86c8a); nanovg's nvgStroke has no such cull.

In wpt-2d-line-miter-acute the path is M100,1000 L100,100 L1000,1000 with stroke-width 200. Its 45-degree miter tip (ratio 2.6131 against limit 2.614) is what covers the 100x50 viewport. The harness maps the SVG at device scale 2z, and the corner's device y is 130+100z: 230 at zoom 1, 255 at 1.25, 280 at 1.5. The corner is the topmost centreline point, so bounds.miny > 260 from zoom 1.3 upward. The whole green stroke is culled and the red background rect shows. That is exactly the zooms that fail: 1.5, 1.75, 2, 3, 4. At zoom 3 and 4 the 59,800 px is the half of the frame the viewport fills.

The miter/bevel decision is correct: cache.rs:1206 tests dmr2*ml^2 < 1, and 2.614^2 * cos^2(67.5 deg) = 1.0007. With the cull fixed, every zoom is 0 px from all three browsers.

Expected behaviour as browsers implement it: Skia's SkCanvas::onDrawPath quick-rejects on paint.computeFastBounds(), which inflates the path bounds by SkStrokeRec::GetInflationRadius (half width times max(miter limit, sqrt2 for square caps)). femtovg's StrokeSettings::reach copies that formula. Firefox draws SVG strokes through Skia (DrawTargetSkia). WebKit hands the stroke to CoreGraphics and does no centreline cull. All three browsers agree pixel for pixel here (chr vs ff = 0 at every failing zoom).

investigations.proposed_issue_title: A stroke whose centreline lies off the canvas is culled even when its width, miter or cap reaches onto it
investigations.fix_sketch:
In stroke_path_internal, move the line_width computation (lib.rs:1621, including the fringe clamp) above the early-out. Then cull on the same inflated bounds that draw_clip already gets: minx - r > width, maxx + r < 0, and likewise for y, with r = stroke.reach(line_width + fringe_width). That is the outer AA edge (half width plus half fringe) times max(miter limit, sqrt2 for square caps), the same as Skia's quick-reject via SkStrokeRec::GetInflationRadius.

The tested patch (stroke-cull-reach.diff) used stroke.reach(width.max(fringe)) + fringe. It is equivalent for every case here, but under-covers the miter-tip fringe by up to (ml/2 - 1) * fringe when ml > 2, so the reach(line_width + fringe) form is the precise one.

Optionally, tighten the reach to half width when the path has no corners, so a straight line is not inflated by the miter limit. The current reach is conservative (10x half width by default), which only costs culling efficiency, not correctness.

Cost: one multiply-add per stroke. No per-draw GPU work and no frame moves outside the 10 explained above (557-render scan).

Sibling to check in the same change: the stroke shadow at lib.rs:1584 bounds the shadow store by centreline ± half width, not by reach (see unproven).

investigations.cluster: morphology -> rename to "usvg-zero-axis-morphology-radius" (usvg resets a zero feMorphology radius on one axis to 1 user unit; resvg#1148). It is one mechanism and all 4 files share it.
investigations.mechanism:
The four files are two SVGs, each present twice (the corpus copy and the wpt22 copy are byte-identical). Each one is `<filter x=0% y=0% width=100% height=100%><feMorphology operator="dilate" radius="15 0"/>` (or "0 15") on a 50x50 rect at (50,50). The filter region is the rect's own box, so the dilation is clipped back to the rect. All that can change is the antialiased edge pixel on each side.

The harness reads the SVG through usvg 0.48.1. In convert_morphology (src/parser/filter.rs:1009-1016) usvg rewrites a zero radius on one axis to 1.0 user unit. Its comment says "this is how Chrome and Safari work", which is not true of current browsers. So the tree the harness gets says radius (15, 1).

The harness maps that to device pixels without changing it (_logos_full.rs:783-786 via FilterSpace::radii, :584-589). At zoom z it hands femtovg ImageFilter::Morphology { radius_x: 15z, radius_y: z }. femtovg rounds a radius to whole pixels the way Skia does (src/filters.rs:192-198), so radius_y = 0.75, 1.25 or 1.75 becomes 1 or 2 px.

At those zooms the rect's top and left edges fall on half pixels: 230 - 50z = 192.5, 167.5, 142.5. The partly covered edge row (or column) on the zero axis has alpha 0.5, and the bogus 1-2 px dilation raises it to 1.0. The harness snaps the filter region outward to whole pixels (scissor_to, _logos_full.rs:875-890, as Blink does), so that row survives. Chromium 131, Firefox and WebKit leave the zero axis alone and keep it at 0.5. That is why the failure is exactly one edge, ceil(50z) px long: 38, 63 and 88 px.

This predicts every zoom with no exceptions:
- At 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4 and 0.5 the edges sit on whole pixels, so the extra dilation is cropped away.
- At 0.33 and 0.25 the edge is a half pixel, but 0.33 and 0.25 round to a 0 px radius.

femtovg is right: with a zero (or near-zero) radius it leaves that axis alone (image.rs:419-421). The browsers agree with each other exactly (chr vs ff = 0 at every failing step). It is not a reference-page artefact either.

investigations.mechanism:
A, zoom 3 (the 7,500 px). Canvas::stroke_path_internal returns early when the path cache's bounds are off the canvas (src/lib.rs:1607-1614). Those bounds are only the flattened centerline points (src/path/cache.rs:349-363), and lib.rs:1573-1574 says so in a comment. At zoom 3 the centerline lands at frame y -35..-5, entirely above the canvas, but the 60 px stroke reaches down to y=25. The early-out drops the whole stroke, so the visible band at y 0..24, x 80..379 (300 x 25 = 7,500 px) stays white while all three browsers draw it green. The same function already works out the stroke's reach, `stroke.reach(line_width)` at lib.rs:1640, and passes it to draw_clip. The shadow path above it (lib.rs:1585-1589) widens the bounds by the half-width. Only the early-out uses the bare centerline. Skia's check does the opposite: SkCanvas::onDrawPath calls internalQuickReject with paint.computeFastBounds, which widens a stroke's bounds by SkStrokeRec::GetInflationRadius (half the width, times the miter limit for miter joins and sqrt2 for square caps). femtovg's StrokeSettings::reach (paint.rs:457-465) uses the same formula. nanovg's nvgStroke has no cull at all; femtovg added this one in 227cb6c1, "Path culling", 2020. The code is in lib.rs, so both backends are affected.

B, zooms 1.25 and 1.75 (26 and 38 px; 0.75 has 18 px, under the 24 px threshold). The butt ends sit on half pixels: x = 167.5/292.5 at zoom 1.25 and 142.5/317.5 at 1.75. In the rows where the two subpaths' strokes overlap, femtovg gives 75 % coverage at the end pixel (64,160,64); the browsers give 50 % (127,191,127). The stencil stroke draws in two passes. The base pass (wgpu.rs:1896-1928) discards fringe fragments below strokeThr. The AA pass (wgpu.rs:1936-1958; OpenGL opengl.rs:695-704) tests stencil == 0 with the KEEP op, so every contour's fringe lands on the same pixel and they blend as 1-(1-a)(1-b). Skia, CoreGraphics and Firefox take the coverage of the union of the outline instead. The same mechanism gives the opposite error where two contours meet end to end: a seam at 75 % where the browsers draw 100 %. Two opaque fringes from one stroke should never compound like this.

investigations.cluster: layer-ctm-drop-shadow, renamed: browsers resample a filter layer kept in user space under rotation. One file: wpt22__19-filter-subregions-and-offcanvas__wpt-2d-layer-ctm-drop-shadow-filter.
investigations.mechanism:
The file fails because all three browsers draw this filtered content inexactly. femtovg's rendering is the accurate one.

**What the browsers do.** Each one rasterizes a filtered element into a layer that follows the element's user space, using only the scale part of the CTM (here 2*zoom). The layer's pixel grid starts at the user origin. The drop-shadow offset is applied in that layer. The layer is then drawn to the device with the remaining part of the CTM, rotate(90) plus a translation, using bilinear filtering.
- In this file the group's user origin lands at device (142.5, 117.5) at zoom 1.25. The rect edges sit at layer coordinates of ±12.5.
- So each rect edge is antialiased once in the layer, and then bilinearly resampled half a pixel off the device grid.
- A rect edge that should land exactly on device x = 130 becomes a two-pixel ramp of 0.25 / 0.75 coverage in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit alike (223 and 160 where femtovg and the exact reference have 255 and 128).
- At zoom 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4 and 0.5 the origin and the layer edges land on whole pixels, and the 90° turn is then an exact pixel permutation. That is why exactly the zooms 1.25, 1.75, 0.75, 0.33 and 0.25 fail.

**What femtovg and the harness do.** The harness draws each filtered element into a femtovg layer stored in device space. The store origin is rounded down to whole pixels (src/budgets.rs:110). The content is rasterized under the full CTM, and the composite copies the store pixel for pixel (src/layers.rs:721). The shadow offset is mapped from user space to the device (harness _logos_full.rs:2694-2697, FilterSpace::vector). So femtovg's grey edges are exact.

**Why femtovg still differs a little from the exact reference.** femtovg composites the shadow at the fractional device offset with bilinear sampling (src/shadow.rs:289 and :310). Chromium makes the same choice: Skia applies feDropShadow's offset with SkFilterMode::kLinear (SkDropShadowImageFilter.cpp:50-54 at chrome/m131). When Chromium's layer happens to line up with the device, it is bit-identical to femtovg (experiment below). By the browser standard this is not a femtovg bug.

**Where the browsers' behaviour comes from:**
- **Chromium (Skia m131):** `Mapping::decomposeCTM` (SkImageFilterTypes.cpp:268-284) keeps only the CTM's scale (via `decompose_transform`, :93-98) when the CTM is not scale+translate. The rotation and translation become a remainder drawn with kDefaultSampling = kLinear (SkImageFilterTypes.h:732). Integer translations are downgraded to nearest; fractional ones are not.
- **Firefox:** `FilterInstance::ComputeUserSpaceToFilterSpaceScale` sets filter space = user space × `mPaintTransform.ScaleFactors()` (layout/svg/FilterInstance.cpp:1609-1626, gecko-dev mirror from July 2025). The result is drawn back under the paint transform.
- **WebKit:** `filterScale` = (absoluteTransform.xScale, yScale), described in the source as eliminating shear (LegacyRenderSVGResourceFilter.cpp:112-120, WebKit main 2a0b8847). The result is drawn back through the context's CTM.

**Two effects that are not this mechanism:**
- Firefox handles the fractional shadow offset differently from Chromium and WebKit. That is the whole Chromium-vs-Firefox difference: 1,344 px at 1.25.
- At zoom 0.33 only, 7 rect-corner pixels where both edges are fractional come out as min(cx, cy) coverage instead of cx*cy. This comes from femtovg's ordinary fringe fill antialiasing and shows up with no filter at all. It is not enough to fail the file.

- **Rotation kept, user origin moved onto whole device pixels** (translate 30.4, 90.4): every browser's rect edges become crisp and equal the area (191 at x = 130), and Chromium is bit-identical to femtovg (0 px).

It rasterizes in a user-aligned layer at scale 2z, applies the shadow offset there bilinearly, crops to the filter region rounded out to layer pixels, and draws to the device with rotate(90) and the fractional translation, bilinear. It matches Chromium within 1/255 at 1.25, 1.75, 0.75 and 0.25, and within 8/255 (0 px beyond) at 0.33. Without the filter-region crop, Chromium's frames differ from the model at the shadow edge that lies on the region boundary.

investigations.cluster: gradient-hard-stops. Suggested rename: "multi-stop-gradient-lut-smears-hard-stops". All 4 files share one cause, and it is a femtovg bug: every gradient with 3 or more stops is drawn through a 256-texel lookup texture with linear filtering, so a hard stop becomes a ramp 1/256 of the gradient length wide.
investigations.mechanism:
femtovg draws a gradient with 3 or more stops in two steps. First it bakes the stops into a 256x1 RGBA8 texture. Then the fragment shader samples that texture at the gradient parameter d with linear filtering. This changes a hard stop in two ways:
(a) Smear: the colour jump between texel e-1 (last yellow) and texel e (first green) becomes a linear ramp between their centres. The ramp is one texel wide, which is L/256 device px for a gradient L px long.
(b) Position shift: e = floor(offset*256) (truncation), so the ramp is centred at floor(offset*256)/256 instead of at the offset. For 0.7 the centre is 179/256 = 0.69922, early by 0.2 texel.

In these files L = 160*zoom px, so the ramp is 0.63 px wide at zoom 1 and 2.5 px at zoom 4. Whenever a pixel centre lands inside it, femtovg writes a yellow/green mix that no browser draws.

This model predicts the frames exactly:
- 0.7 files, zoom 4: ramp centre 357.5, width 2.5 px, so cols 356/357/358 should have R = 229.5/127.5/25.5. femtovg has 229/128/26.
- 0.7 files, zoom 2: col 293 should have R = 178.5. femtovg has 178.
- zero-offset file, zoom 4: the stop is exactly on texel 128, so the ramp is centred on the true stop at x=230 with half-width 0.3125*zoom px. It reaches a pixel centre only when zoom > 1.6, which is exactly why that file fails only at 1.75, 2, 3 and 4, always in 2 columns. Predicted R at cols 229/230 is 178.5/76.5; femtovg has 178/76.

The browsers evaluate the gradient function at each pixel centre, so a hard stop stays a one-pixel step. Skia m131 raster (Chromium --disable-gpu; Firefox frames are pixel-identical here):
- STAGE(gradient), src/opts/SkRasterPipeline_opts.h:3466-3476, picks the interval as the count of t >= ts[i].
- gradient_lookup, :3454-3457, computes the colour as t*f+b.
- The setup in src/shaders/gradients/SkGradientBaseShader.cpp:431-455 skips zero-length intervals (`if (t_l < t_r)`, :440).

Skia's GPU path (Ganesh, src/gpu/ganesh/gradients/GrGradientShader.cpp:548-591) is analytic for up to 128 stops: dual-interval, unrolled or looping binary-search colorizers on uniforms. It uses a 256-texel texture (kGradientTextureSize = 256, :79) only as a fallback, and its own comment at :892-893 says the texture technique "always blurs hard-stops". femtovg uses that fallback for every gradient with 3 or more stops. WebKit (CoreGraphics) agrees with Chromium and Firefox at zooms 1 to 4.

Not the harness:
- The harness passes usvg's stops through unchanged (_logos_full.rs:64-74, 90-92).
- usvg 0.48.1 turns equal or decreasing offsets into (offset - f32::EPSILON, offset) (parser/paint_server.rs:374-396). That keeps the hard stop.
- The master binary reproduces the ladder counts exactly.

Not the reference pages: all three browsers agree, and so does the area reference.

investigations.fix_sketch:
Evaluate the stops per fragment, as Skia does, instead of baking them into a filtered texture.
- Per gradient, store a small stop table: for each non-empty interval, its threshold t_i and a per-channel scale and bias (f_i, b_i) in straight (unpremultiplied) space, so #326/#363 behaviour is kept. Skip zero-length intervals, as SkGradientBaseShader.cpp:440 does. That is what makes hard stops exact.
- Fragment: idx = number of t_i <= d, using a bounded loop with break so GLSL ES 1.00 can compile it; colour = d*f[idx] + b[idx]; then premultiply and dither as now.
- Storage on wgpu: an Rgba32Float row read with textureLoad (no filtering), or a storage buffer.
- Storage on GL: RGBA32F where available. For GLES2/WebGL1, pack t_i into two 8-bit channels (1/65536 precision) and read texel centres with NEAREST.
- Packing all of a frame's gradients into one atlas row-per-gradient would also do what the TODO at gradient_store.rs:12-13 asks.
- Keep it in the existing FillImageGradient, conic and two-point-radial shader variants, so draws without a gradient pay nothing. The loop costs about one compare per stop (3 here).
- This also removes the two sub-threshold side effects of the current texture: the half-texel lag of ordinary colour ramps (each texel holds the colour at i/N but is drawn at (i+0.5)/N, 1.25 px at zoom 4 here) and the truncating `as u8` at :105-108.

Not proposed:
- A wider texture is a band-aid. The ramp is L/N px wide and grows with zoom; N=1024 still fails at zooms 3 and 4.
- NEAREST filtering alone is not enough either: the stop is still quantised to floor(o*N)/N, and nearest-256 still fails at zoom 4.
- A WebRender-style table of per-entry start and end colours keeps hard stops sharp but still snaps stop positions to 1/N.

The fix needs paired cost A/B runs on both backends (per the memory notes on shader variants and per-draw bindings). I did not measure that.

Both files fail only at zoom 0.33, and both come from one femtovg fill design with two faces. (a) makeup page_275_icon_24: rings drawn as an outer contour plus a convex hole, walls 1.13 px wide at 0.33. The #408 gate calls them convex, so they keep the fringe and come out 11-23% too dark. (b) shoe page_70_icon_17: pixel art drawn as one path of abutting 8 px squares. Every edge two contours share leaves a seam with only 0.75+d^2 coverage. investigations.mechanism:
How femtovg fills a path with more than one contour (ConcaveFill, both backends):
- The stencil fan of every contour is pulled half a pixel into the solid side of its edge. For a hole contour that side is the ring's wall.
- Each contour then gets its own full fringe: a 2 px strip running from 1.5 px inside the edge (alpha 0) through 0.5 px inside (alpha 1) to 0.5 px outside (alpha 0).
- Each strip is drawn src-over wherever that shrunken stencil is still 0.
- Only a path with exactly one convex contour takes ConvexFill, with half a fringe and no overlap.

(a) Edges that face each other less than about 2 px apart get both strips over the same pixels, so they over-ink. This is the #327 mechanism. #408 added a gate meant to send such fills through exact-area masks: a fill is thin if its mean width is under 2 px, or under 1 px if "convex". But PathCache::mean_width sets convex when each contour is convex, not when the fill is a single convex contour. So a ring made of two convex contours gets the 1 px limit while it is still drawn with the full fringe. Walls between 1 and about 1.6 px wide are never masked and over-ink:
- 1D model of the fringe: 1.19x at 1.13 px, 1.03x at 1.5 px, 1.004x at 1.72 px.
- Measured per ring path at 0.33: 1.11-1.23x the area. Chromium is 0.98-1.09x; WebKit is about 1.00x.

(b) Where two contours of one path share an edge, both stencils stop 0.5 px short of it. That leaves a 1 px band at stencil 0, and both contours' fringes are drawn there. A pixel whose centre is d px from the shared edge ends up with coverage 1-(0.5-d)(0.5+d) = 0.75+d^2 instead of 1. Browsers instead work out the coverage of the whole path's winding (Skia's scan converter for Chromium and Firefox, CoreGraphics for WebKit), so an edge inside the union adds nothing.

Why only zoom 0.33 fails:
- Shoe: one square is 40.96 x 200/1024 = 8 px at zoom 1. Edges sit at x = 230 + (8k-100)·z, which is a whole pixel at every ladder zoom except 0.33 (197 + 2.64k). With d = 0.5, coverage is 1 and there is no seam.
- Makeup: walls are 1.13 px at 0.33. At 0.25 they are 0.86 px, under the 1 px limit, so they are masked and exact. At 0.5 they are 1.72 px, where over-ink is 0.4%.

investigations.mechanism: (A) File 1. femtovg antialiases a fill or stroke with a ramp along the distance to the nearest edge, and it samples that ramp once, at the pixel centre. The ramp runs 1 px wide: for a convex fill, inner vertex u=0.5 and outer vertex u=1; the shader computes min(1,(1-|2u-1|)*stroke_mult). The quads of two edges meet on the miter diagonal. So at a convex corner a pixel takes min(ramp_x, ramp_y), and at a concave corner (the inner corner of a stroked frame) it takes max. The area would be the product, or 1-(1-a)(1-b) for the concave case. With the corner on a fraction f of a pixel, femtovg draws 1-f where the area is (1-f)^2. The error is f(1-f): up to 64/255 at f=0.5, and above 8/255 for every f between 0.03 and 0.97. Chromium, Firefox and WebKit all give the area: in the repro, Chromium 1x matches the 8x area reference to within 0.003 at every f. Chromium and Firefox are pixel-identical in this file at every zoom (both Skia); WebKit is CoreGraphics. At zooms 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4 and 0.5 every rect edge lands on a whole pixel. At 1.25, 1.75, 0.75 and 0.25 the edges land on x.5, and at 0.33 on other fractions. Each failing step is the 48 rect-corner pixels, plus 0-12 frame-corner pixels where the 1 px frame's corners are on screen. (B) File 2, stroke-dasharray="40 0". femtovg's dasher gives every dash its own subpath (move_to/line_to). Each dash gets a butt cap whose ramp is 0.5 at the end point. The Stroke command then draws each subpath's triangle strip as its own draw with source-over blending and no stencil. Where two dashes meet with no gap, the seam pixel therefore gets 1-(0.5-t)(0.5+t) = 0.75+t^2 instead of 1, where t is the seam's offset from the pixel centre. Skia emits each dash as a contour of one path (SkDashPath::InternalFilter, getSegment(...,true)), strokes that path, and fills the result once with nonzero winding. CG behaves the same as observed. Either way the union has no seam. The seams sit at 230±20z, which is a whole pixel at every ladder zoom except 0.33 (223.4 / 236.6). So file 2 fails only at 0.33: 56 of its 60 px against WebKit are seams, and the other 4 are frame corners (mechanism A). The cause is not specific to the dasher: one path made of two abutting subpaths, with no dash, gives 0.749 in femtovg and 1.0 in Chromium. investigations.fix_sketch: (A) First, upright rect fills: the path_fill_is_rect / RectFill case, axis-aligned under the transform. Draw them as one quad whose coverage is clamp(cover_x)*clamp(cover_y), the box coverage femtovg already evaluates for clip boxes (shader.wgsl:409-410) and the scissor (385-386). That is the exact area at any fractional position, and the fringe strip goes away. An upright stroked rect with miter joins is the outer box minus the inner box, which would fix the WPT frame's 8 px. General convex fills keep min-of-ramps at corners. Possible routes there: multiply the two edges' ramps in the miter wedge (exact at right angles; it needs both distances as varyings), extend the #408 masks, or adopt exact coverage (#13/#358, which was dropped for cost). Any of these must be measured against the median frame-time budget. Also correct the is_thin doc comment, which claims the fringe draws a rectangle exactly. (B) The root fix is union coverage for one stroke, as Skia does it: stroke the dashes into a single outline and fill it once with nonzero winding. In femtovg that means taking multi-subpath strokes whose subpaths touch through the stencil-winding or coverage path, or accumulating the command's coverage additively, clamped to 1, and resolving it. Both are exact for abutting disjoint pieces. A dasher-local change is exact for this file and proven here (60 -> 4): in dash_line_segment, continue the subpath with line_to when a dash starts where the previous one ended on the same chord. It belongs with #417's 'keep a dash one subpath' change in the same function. It must not join across a vertex, because Chromium and WebKit leave the corners unjoined, and it does not cover authored abutting subpaths. Do not adopt Firefox's ContinuousStroke rule: it would fill the corner squares and break agreement with Chromium and WebKit.

(a) "three-box-reference", 30 files: Chromium and Firefox approximate feGaussianBlur with the SVG spec's three successive box blurs, and femtovg draws the actual Gaussian. investigations.mechanism:
(a) femtovg's blur is a Gaussian. Each pass uses true Gaussian weights at the integer taps from -(ceil(3σ)-1) to +(ceil(3σ)-1), normalised to sum to 1. Above σ 8 the image is halved, blurred and scaled back up. At device σ 2 this is within 3/255 of the analytic, pixel-integrated Gaussian, which is the spec's normative kernel.

Chromium 131 renders feGaussianBlur on its raster path with Skia's old ("legacy") blur code, which always uses the successive box blur. The SkUserConfig.h define SK_USE_LEGACY_BLUR_RASTER makes getBlurEngine() return null, and SkBlurImageFilter then hard-wires GaussPass, which runs three box blurs of width d = floor(σ·3√(2π)/4 + 0.5).

At device σ 2, d rounds up from 3.76 to 4, which is even. The spec's even case is two boxes of 4 plus one of 5, giving variance 4.5 against the Gaussian's 4: the kernel is 6 % too wide. Each one-dimensional edge profile is then about 3/255 off the Gaussian on the side opposite to femtovg's own 3/255 rounding. At a blurred rect's corners the two axis profiles multiply, so the two errors add to 9-11/255 on 8-9 px per corner. That makes 32 px (36 px for σ 3,2, where the x window d=6 has the same even-rounding overshoot), just over the 24 px criterion.

Firefox 159 sends the same blur through Skia's raster blur and matches Chromium to 1/255 here. So the two "agreeing" references are one implementation, not two independent confirmations.

bigblur at zoom 3 (device σ 75 / 56 / 37.5) is the same thing at large σ: the boxes come out about 6 % narrower than the Gaussian. The difference is a smooth one of at most 10/255 that happens to cross 8/255 on 40 px.

(b) The file draws a red rect, blurs it inside a filter region equal to its bbox, clips it to the same rect, then covers it with a green rect on exactly the same edges. At zoom 0.33 those edges fall at x 206.9 / 239.9 and y 106.9 / 139.9.

Each step, checked alone, matches a reference:
- The blur with no clip: femtovg and Chromium both round the filter region out to whole pixels, and agree with each other to 0 px.
- The clip with no cover: femtovg's antialiased clip equals the 8x area reference to 0 px. Chromium's rect clip-path is aliased: the pixel with 0.1 coverage gets no red and the pixel with 0.9 coverage gets all of it, which puts it 117 px off the area reference.

Put together, the rounded-out red at the 0.1-covered left and top edges is scaled by femtovg's 0.1 clip coverage. The green's 0.1 antialiased edge then lets it show through, which is conflation. Chromium's aliased clip has already removed that red, so it shows no leak on those two edges. On the right and bottom edges both engines leak, Chromium more. WebKit antialiases its clips the way femtovg does and leaks on all four edges.

The analytic answer has no red anywhere. Against it femtovg is 116 px off, Chromium 63 and WebKit 131. Chromium and WebKit differ from each other by 117 px, more than femtovg differs from either (52 from Chromium, 66 from WebKit).

The only femtovg-specific part is 2 corner pixels from its convex-fill fringe. At a corner pixel the fringe gives about the smaller of the two edge coverages, not their product: 0.1×0.1 is drawn as 0.1 and 0.9×0.9 as 0.9. That is under the threshold here (2 px, max 24) and is the general fringe limitation covered by #13.

investigations.mechanism:
(A) lists-empty-state-light. Two femtovg stroker defects, plus one zoom where the browsers disagree.

A1, a new bug (red crescents at the inner ends of the pill outlines, femtovg puts down more ink than the reference). The cause is calculate_joins' inner-bevel test, inherited from nanovg: limit = max(1.01, min(len0,len1)/W); INNERBEVEL is set if dmr2*limit^2 < 1, where W is half the stroke width plus half the fringe. Whenever a chord is shorter than about W, this bevels every turn sharper than 16.2 degrees (cos(theta/2) < 1/1.01). The test compares the inner miter's length W/cos(theta/2) with the chord. What actually matters is how far the miter point's foot lies along the chord, W*tan(theta/2).

Worked example: the pill's end at zoom 1.75 has W = 3.68 px and flattened chords of about 2.5 px turning 22.5 degrees. Every point is flagged INNERBEVEL, yet the foot is only 0.73 px, under half a chord (1.25 px), so a miter would not fold. On a bevel, choose_bevel puts the inner side at each chord's own perpendicular offset, so neighbouring quads overlap on the inside of the curve. The stencil stroke's core pass draws each pixel once (IncrementClamp). The AA pass, however, uses pass_op Keep, so every fringe fragment where the stencil is still 0 is blended. Overlapping fringes therefore give 1-(1-a0)(1-a1) instead of the union's coverage. The pill's hole loses about 0.2 px at its end: grey 196-201 where the area reference has 208-215, on a 192..251 ramp.

A2, issue #421 (blue dots at the checkboxes' outer corners, too little ink). The squares use stroke-linejoin round at width 2. round_join gives a 90-degree turn only 3 points, so the chords cut up to about 0.24 px inside the arc.

A3, zoom 0.25 only: the strokes are 0.91 px wide. Chromium under-inks them and WebKit over-inks them (Chromium vs WebKit: 52 px). femtovg is the nearest renderer to the area reference (13 px, or 9 with both fixes) while Chromium, Firefox and WebKit are 32-34 px off. This is a genuine browser disagreement.

(B) wallpaper-landscape-planet, fills and gradients only (no strokes).

B1, the harness mapping, shared with the browsers: clip-path "a" coincides with the viewport. The harness applies clip-path and viewport clips per draw (it does not set CLIP_GROUP_LAYERS by default), so each of about 4 stacked fills takes the clip's coverage at the bottom edge and the lower layers bleed through. That is the known "stacked draws under one antialiased clip edge" class. At zoom 0.25 the bottom row computes to (244.7, 237.5, 250.4) by hand; femtovg gives (245,237,250) and the area reference (253,252,253). femtovg's bottom row equals Chromium's at 9 of 10 zooms (identical px counts off the area). Exact results need the clipped group drawn into one layer.

- At zoom 1.75, Chromium and Firefox draw the bottom row at full coverage.

- WebKit multiplies the opacity layer's bounding clip with the horizon fill's own edge at y=596 (detailed under evidence).

B3, femtovg's own residual: 0-15 px on the planet arc. This is the flattening tolerance (TESS_TOL 0.125, chords straddling the curve) and is under the threshold on its own.

investigations.mechanism:
All 25 files draw the same resvg "image frame": <rect x=1 y=1 width=198 height=198 stroke=black>, a 1-unit stroke at fit 1. At zoom 0.25, 0.33 and 0.75 it becomes a 0.25, 0.33 or 0.75 px line. At 0.5 and 1 it lands centred on a pixel or a pixel boundary, where every model agrees, so those zooms pass.

femtovg draws a stroke thinner than the fringe at the fringe width (1 px) and multiplies its alpha by w (lib.rs:1623-1635, linear since #339). The stroke mask min(1, (1-|2u-1|)*stroke_mult) with stroke_mult = 1 is then a 2 px tent at peak w, sampled at pixel centres. The total ink is right, but the coverage is spread by where the centreline falls. Measured on the top edge, femtovg vs the exact area:
- 0.25 px: 0.188 vs 0.25
- 0.33 px: 0.275 vs 0.33. The tent's other 0.056 goes into the row outside the viewport, which the viewport clip removes.
- 0.75 px: 0.561/0.188 vs 0.625/0.125

That is 14-16/255 on every pixel of the frame (196 / 260 / 1184 px).

The browsers split three ways:
- Chromium paints an SVG <rect> stroke with GraphicsContext::DrawRect (svg_shape_painter.cc StrokeShape, kRectangle case). Skia's SkDrawBase::drawRect then takes ComputeRectType -> kStroke_RectType -> SkScan::AntiFrameRect, which is exact area (src/core/SkDrawBase.cpp:111-132, 233-235 at chrome/m131).
- The same frame as a <path> goes through drawPath. There SkDrawTreatAsHairline swaps in a 1 px hairline at alpha = w (SkDrawBase.cpp:420-437; SkDrawTreatAAStrokeAsHairline at 262), which is exactly femtovg's profile.
- Firefox 159 is exact for both rect and path (measured). DrawTargetSkia::StrokeRect calls drawRect; why its drawPath is also exact is not traced.
- WebKit (Core Graphics) draws the hairline-like profile for both, matching femtovg to 1/255.

So on the frame the browsers disagree with each other by the whole frame (Chromium vs WebKit 1176 px at 0.75), while femtovg disagrees with the nearest browser (WebKit) by 4-12 px. By the maintainer's rule this is a genuine browser disagreement. Against the area reference (ground truth), femtovg is off on the whole frame and Chromium and Firefox are exact.

Each file fails because no single browser matches femtovg everywhere:
- Chromium and Firefox fail it on the frame.
- WebKit fails it elsewhere, on WebKit-only differences: its filter/flood region starts a pixel early (the feblend mode= files: 100/301 px on the frame band), and isolation, blend and filter-region pixels where WebKit differs from both Chromium and Firefox by about femtovg's count.

Separate mechanisms:
- (a) resvg-feblend/empty at 0.33: a harness artefact. The filter is <feBlend/> with in = in2 = SourceGraphic, so the browsers composite the source over itself (alpha a + a(1-a); an edge pixel at 0.4 becomes 0.645). A CPU-only change in stroke_path_internal (src/lib.rs:1623-1690); no shader change, so GL and wgpu both get it through the shared Params.

For an antialiased stroke with 0 < w < fringe f:
- keep the alpha scale w/f (#339);
- stop widening: pass the true w to expand_stroke(w*0.5, f, ...), so the geometry reaches w/2 + f/2;

investigations.mechanism:
(A) femtovg, small and already known. clipMask takes coverage inside a round corner as clamp(0.5 - signed distance). That is a pixel's exact share only where the edge runs along an axis. On a 45-degree edge the box-filter area is quadratic near the pixel's corners, so the ramp is up to 0.043 off, which is 11/255 at full contrast. The max error is 9-13/255 at every zoom, so roughly 1 in 8 diagonal edge pixels crosses 8/255. The count grows with the circumference, which is why the failures appear at 1.25-4x. The analytic fit itself is exact: it fits the true ellipse through usvg's cubics, and a 16-arc input renders bit-for-bit the same.

Most failures in A are not femtovg's alone. They add WebKit's own sub-threshold errors, which sit elsewhere on the circle: WebKit errs on the near-axis stretches at 1.5-2x (60-68 px beyond 8/255 of the exact area, where femtovg has 16-52 px). Every browser is further from the exact area than femtovg except WebKit.

(B) Harness/usvg geometry, not femtovg. usvg converts both <circle> and path arcs into cubics at a fixed 0.1 user-unit tolerance. kurbo's segment count bottoms out at 4 per full turn, so every circle under about 367 units of radius is four 90-degree cubics. Each cubic (kappa = 4/3 tan(pi/8)) bulges outward by up to 2.7e-4 r, peaking 18.9 and 71.1 degrees into each segment. At 3x the ring's radius is about 199 px, so the bulge is 0.054 px, which on a 2.5 px ring is 16/255. The coverage mask is an exact-area CPU rasteriser, and it draws exactly that geometry. The analytic shapes in A do not show the bulge, because the fit drops it (shape.rs documents the 0.03 % stray). WebKit and Firefox show the same bulge profile: they also draw cubics. Chromium draws no bulge, but software Chromium shrinks the edge by 0.04-0.11 px.

(C) femtovg. The mask rasteriser sums signed areas per cell and only then folds by the fill rule. In a pixel that holds windings 0, 1 and 2 (the five inner vertices of a self-crossing even-odd pentagram), the fold gives a1 + 2*a2 instead of a1. That over-covers by up to 60/255 at 1.25x and 86/255 at 1.75x. #407 fixed nested even-odd contours by rewinding them, but that cannot help a contour that crosses itself. At 2-4x the failures in this file are WebKit's own error (44-115 px from the area, against femtovg's 3-4).

investigations.cluster: feoffset: rename it "fractional device offsets: each engine resamples them its own way". The 57 entries are 29 files; 28 of them appear in both corpora, and offset-circle-shape is only in corpus__. They split three ways. A: 52 entries, a browser disagreement on how to resample an feOffset whose device shift is fractional. B: 4 entries, a harness mapping gap where the chain never runs. C: 1 entry, curve antialiasing, nothing to do with feOffset.
investigations.mechanism:
A (52 entries, browser disagreement). When dx·zoom·scale is not a whole number of device pixels, the offset image has to be resampled. Each engine does this differently, and none of them reproduces the exact coverage:
- femtovg samples bilinearly. This is documented and deliberate since #374.
- Chromium (Skia m131) samples nearest-neighbour and then draws the image with antialiased bounds, which leaves a sliver at the shifted boundary.
- Firefox truncates the offset to a whole filter-space pixel with an int32_t cast.
- WebKit draws the input ImageBuffer at the fractional rect through CoreGraphics interpolation.
So every failing pixel sits on an edge that the offset moved. The ladder fails only at zooms where the device shift is fractional (0.33, 0.75, 1.25, 1.75). At zoom 1 with pixel-aligned sources, femtovg, Chromium and WebKit all agree (bilinear and nearest-plus-AA-bounds are both exact there); only Firefox's truncation differs.
- offset-border-stroke-fill has a second difference on top. Chromium does not clip SourceGraphic to the filter region, so its stroke band is twice as wide. Firefox and WebKit do clip it, and the harness follows them (#337 already records this).
- The chained-* files differ the same way at each step. femtovg folds the two shifts into one bilinear tap; the browsers resample at every step.

B (4 entries, harness artefact). The harness cannot map two chains:
- offset-triple-chain-rgb-shadow: feMerge of s2, s1 and SourceGraphic. Only [previous, SourceGraphic] is mapped.
- offset-sourcealpha-flood: feOffset(SourceAlpha), then feFlood, then feComposite in, then feMerge. shadow_chain demands an feGaussianBlur, and layer_chain stops at feFlood.

In both cases the chain is dropped, and the group draws its source alone under the rounded-out filter-region scissor. At zoom 1 the offset copies sit exactly under the source, so the frame still matches. At fractional zooms the browsers' copies fill the partial edge pixel of the rounded-out region, which femtovg never draws. Expressed in a form the harness does map, femtovg matches all three browsers.

C (1 entry, not feOffset). offset-circle-shape at zoom 3 has integer device offsets (120, 90). The failure is the circle's arc antialiasing at r = 90 px.

Side observation (4 px per rect, below threshold on its own): femtovg fills a rect's corner pixel with min(a, b) of the two edge coverages instead of a·b. For example 0.40 where the exact value is 0.16.

investigations.mechanism:
Two femtovg defects in the convex fringe meet at each 0.716 deg corner. The corners are points (-10,130) and (470,130) at zoom 3, both flagged CORNER|LEFT|BEVEL.

At zoom 1 to 2 the fill goes through #408's exact-area mask, because its mean width is z/2, under 1. From zoom 3 the mean width is 1.5 or more, so the convex fringe path draws it (lib.rs:1351, clip/fill.rs:20).

(1) expand_fill tests `p1.flags.contains(PointFlags::BEVEL | PointFlags::INNERBEVEL)` (cache.rs:998). That needs BOTH flags. nanovg's nvg__expandFill tests `flags & (BEVEL|INNERBEVEL)`, which needs either. e52ab3ea (2020) made the switch; be1bf333 restored it for strokes only. So a corner past the miter limit, without INNERBEVEL, takes the miter branch: it emits p + dm*lw and p - dm*rw instead of bevel_join. INNERBEVEL is set only while dmr2*min(len)^2 < 1: at zoom 1 here, not at zoom 2 and above.

(2) calculate_joins caps the miter scale: `(1.0 / dmr2).min(600.0)` (cache.rs:1172, the same cap as in nanovg). For a 0.716 deg corner the true miter is 1/sin(theta/2) = 160; capped, |dm| = 3.75. The fill's inset vertex (cache.rs:953) and both fringe vertices therefore sit 1.875 px from the corner instead of 80 px. The dump from an instrumented build shows fill (468.125, 130.012) and outer stroke vertex (471.875, 129.988).

Result: each edge's fringe quad is 1 px wide at the apex and about 0.03 px wide at the corner. Its outer line meets the true edge there. Coverage jumps from 0 to 1 across a sliver, so most of both long edges is sampled at pixel centres. At zoom 3, row 130 stays blank for x < 23 where the area is 33-97/255. It then jumps to 255 at x = 39, where the area is about 190/255.

Fixing (1) alone (nanovg parity) is not enough. The capped inset still puts alpha 1 almost onto the edges near the corners: +58 px of ink at zoom 3, 299 px still beyond 8/255 against WebKit. Fixing (2) alone would push the outer vertex 80 px past the corner.

Browsers: Chromium and Firefox are identical (0 px beyond 8/255 between them). Both are 332-344 px off the area (max 31/255). WebKit matches the exact area within 3/255. The browsers do disagree, but femtovg (403 px, max 109/255 against the nearest, WebKit) is far outside that spread. So the failure is femtovg's. The harness maps this file to a plain canvas.fill_path, and the reference page is correct.
